about: The invocation that closes the prayers of Leo XIII, added to them by Pius X in 1904 and said three times. The first line carries no verb at all — a title held up, and the answer comes only after it. Latin kept the Greek declension of the Holy Name, Iesus, Iesu, Iesum, so the form Iesu is genitive, dative, ablative and vocative at once — the ablative being Latin's own addition, for Greek has no such case — and only the sense decides which.

w001.function: A nominative doing the work of a vocative, as “Agnus” does in the Agnus Dei; a neuter would not show the difference here in any case.

w002.function: Genitive — whose Heart. The same form could be dative, ablative or vocative: the name declines in the Greek way and does not tell them apart.

w003.function: The superlative of sacrátus, consecrated; it agrees in gender with “Cor” (w001), not with the name standing nearer to it.

w004.function: The imperative of a deponent verb: passive in form, active in meaning.

w005.function: Dative. Classical Latin gives this verb a genitive; the liturgy says “miserére nobis”, and that is what stayed.
